The Haṃsa Upaniṣad. Peace: "That is full. The extreme secrecy of the Haṃsa-knowledge, which is the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman.
Gautama said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all scriptures, by what means indeed does the awakening of the knowledge of Brahman arise? (1)
Sanatkumāra said:
O Gautama, having deliberated upon all dharmas and understood the intention of the wielder of the Pināka bow, Pārvatī spoke the truth; listen to that from me.
This secret, which is like a treasure-trove, is inexpressible; it is the expansion of the form of the *haṃsa*, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the yogin. (3)
The commentary:
I am that splendor which is pure Brahman, the supportless foundation where the channel of *nāda*— as described in the *Haṃsa Upaniṣad*— comes to rest.

Indeed, regarding this *Haṃsa Upaniṣad*, since it is a subdivision of the Śukla Yajurveda, the introductory remarks found in the *Īśāvāsya*, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, and other texts should be understood here as well.
This narrative takes the form of a dialogue consisting of questions by Sanatkumāra and Gautama and their respective answers.

(p. 560) This [section] is for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*). In that regard, it is first stated that Gautama asks Sanatkumāra about the knowledge of Brahman and its means: "O Blessed One" (*bhagavan*), etc.
O Blessed One, endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers (*ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya*), knower of all dharmas, and proficient in all scriptures—thus [he addresses him].
By these three addresses: "You are omniscient because you have ascended to the state of being the Lord of the Omniscient;

therefore, out of compassion, please teach that means by which the awakening of the knowledge of Brahman—the realization of nothing but the non-dual Brahman—may arise for me instantly and without effort. (1) Thus.
When Sanatkumāra, the sage, was questioned by Gautama, he spoke these words—praising the knowledge about to be taught—in order to inspire the listener’s intellect; thus it is said: "Sanatkumāra said.
"O Gautama, that which is the conviction of the Lord of All, the wielder of the Pināka bow—a conviction free from all mental constructions other than the Self—"

Having understood from the very mouth of that [scripture] that "Brahman is only the Self," one should then maintain the realization that Brahman is pure Being (sanmātra), established through the negation of all that is unreal and distinct from oneself; this is the dharma to be upheld in those Vedānta texts wherein it is maintained as the universal dharma.

Having thoroughly investigated and ascertained [the truth] within the one hundred and eight Upanishads beginning with the *Īśa*, Pārvatī— who is the very essence of the world and the embodiment of Brahma-vidyā— out of her pure grace taught me that reality of Brahman; therefore, with a mind focused and attentive, [one should contemplate] that doctrine which is favored by the wielder of the Pināka bow.

Listen; the meaning is: having heard, grasp it correctly. To the question "Of what nature is that?", he says: "It is inexpressible. He says "it is inexpressible" (anākhyeyam) to indicate that this knowledge of Brahman which I am about to declare is secret and must be concealed from those who are not yogis. Never...
The meaning is that it must be spoken [only to the qualified]. Regarding the fact that great harm would arise from proclaiming this to those who are not qualified, it is said:
"He who says to the ignorant or the half-awakened, 'Everything is Brahman,' by that act he consigns them to the empire of the great hells."
One should not create a division of thought in the ignorant who are attached to knowledge.
And thus, the Śruti and Smṛti are the authority. If so, to whom should this be told? To this he says: "to the yogin.
A yogin is one who is endowed with the means for the application of the knowledge of Brahman, preceded by the conduct of his own stage of life (āśrama);
it is to such a yogin that this should be spoken by the teacher—this is the meaning. Of what nature is that [knowledge]?

Regarding what fruit it yields, he says: "Of the Haṃsa. The Haṃsa is the Supreme Self (paramātman), so called because by the awakening of its own nature alone, it destroys—that is, performs the negation (apahnava)—of all conceptualizations other than itself. Its expansion of form consists of the Viśva, Virāṭ, Otrā, and so forth; that very Brahman is like a treasury of the jewels of knowledge.

The liberation from one's own ignorance is the negation of that which is other than oneself; that which bestows the fruit thereof—namely, the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) characterized by abiding as one's own true nature—is what I am about to speak; listen to it. This is the connection with the preceding verse. || 3 ||

(p. 561) Now we shall explain the determination of the Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa, which is the essential nature of the master of the Haṃsa-vidyā; [this is for] the celibate student who is self-controlled and devoted to the guru, who constantly meditates on "Haṃsa, Haṃsa. (4)

In response to the inquiry as to what the expansion of the form of the Haṃsa is, who its qualified practitioner is, what the fruit of that knowledge is, and what its means of accomplishment are, the Sage, having found a suitable candidate, explains all of this with the word "atha" (now). Now.

Immediately after the attainment of the qualifications as described, one destroys the three states beginning with waking in succession and proceeds to the state of the Fourth (*turya*); thus, the *haṃsa* is the individual Fourth, the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
That very same [self] is the supreme, most excellent universal Fourth, which, having destroyed the three collective states, is that state of the Fourth.

"He goes," thus [is defined] the Paramahaṃsa. We shall clearly explain—the term "explain" (ākhyāsyāmaḥ) meaning we shall state—the determination of the true nature of these two, the Haṃsa and the Paramahaṃsa, which are the inner and the outer; that is, the knowledge of the distinction between the inner and the outer, their unity, and their non-duality as Brahman alone. To what kind of qualified seeker will you speak? Regarding this:

The repetition "haṃsaḥ haṃsaḥ" is for the purpose of [realizing] "I am He. He who, preceded by such constant contemplation that "He is I," meditates upon His true nature, moves within Brahman—that is, desires to ascend to the state of being established in Brahman—he is a *brahmacārī*; for that *brahmacārī*...
"To you who are self-controlled, whose collection of faculties has been brought under mastery, who are devoted to the Guru who teaches the ultimate truth,
and who have faith in the meaning taught by the Guru— we shall explain"— this is the connection with what precedes. || 4 ||

That which has the nature of the *haṃsa* and is the fruit of that knowledge exists pervading all bodies, just as fire is in wood or oil in sesame seeds; having known it, one does not meet with death. || 5 ||

Regarding the question of what delimits that *haṃsa* and where it ought to have its seat, he states this with an illustration: "In all... Just as fire exists pervading the wood—both its own concealers and its own fuel—and just as oil exists in sesame seeds, so too [does the *haṃsa*].

It exists pervading all bodies from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, which are attached to the vision of one's own ignorance, appearing in the forms of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as the direct (pratyak) and the remote (para)— serving as the substrates for the superimposition and negation of those [attributes].
When one's own ignorance is destroyed through the knowledge of oneself...

p. 562) Due to the absence of pervasiveness—which is dependent upon being pervaded—nothing but the non-dual Brahman alone remains, which is devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*). He states the fruit of knowing that [Brahman] with the word "him" (*tam*):
having known Him thus, at the very moment of that knowledge, one does not go toward death, which is the delusion regarding the existence of anything other than oneself.
The meaning is that the wise one remains as the Brahman alone, established through the negation of everything other than Himself. 5. Yoga is the means for attaining the knowledge of the Haṃsa;
having restrained the anus and raised the vital air from the *ādhāra*, [one should lead it] three times to the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.

Having circumambulated [the heart] and gone to Maṇipūraka, having transcended Anāhata, one reaches the two [centers] resembling the penis. Having restrained the vital breaths in Viśuddhi and proceeding toward Ājñā while meditating upon the aperture of Brahmā, one should always contemplate: "I am the three measures."
And he sees without form. This is that Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), resembling ten million suns, by whom all this is pervaded.
Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to what the means for attaining right knowledge is,

he teaches Yoga as that very means, beginning with the words "having pressed the anus. From the statement, "Having known That, one does not meet death," it is understood that the attainment of Brahman, which swallows death, results from knowing [It] alone.

For some whose minds are impure, even though they possess the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), the knowledge of Brahman—which swallows death—does not arise merely from hearing the Vedānta. In that case, the obstacle is the impurity of the mind.
If that is purified by the pure water called Yoga, then the very knowledge previously heard [from scripture] [will bear fruit].

Having abandoned the appearance of its own nature, it attains the state of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Consequently, simultaneously with that perfect knowledge, the attainment of Brahman—which is the devouring of death—is desired. Therefore, the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) should be practiced as a means of knowledge for the purpose of attaining Brahman.

What is this eight-limbed yoga? It consists of the eight limbs: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). Having practiced these correctly in the presence of a teacher, one should then, for the sake of absorption, enter a cave free from the crowding of people.
Having entered [the practice], the yogi, seated in the Siddhāsana posture, presses the anus with the left ankle,

fills the breath through both nostrils or the mouth, and having retained it (kumbhaka), raises the vital air from the Mūlādhāra by means of perfect contraction, thereby achieving the unification of Prāṇa and Apāna.
Having done this, he unites the fire located in the triangle of the *mūlādhāra* with the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, awakens the *kuṇḍalinī*, and through her,
pierces the *brahmagranthi*— the door-panel of the *suṣumnā* situated in the *mūlādhāra*— which is endowed with four petals.
Having entered the *mūlādhāra* cakra and meditated upon the *virāj* or the fourth state (*turya*),
one then circumambulates three times the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, which is adorned with six petals;
then, having gone to the *maṇipūraka*, which is adorned with ten spokes, one reaches the *anāhata* cakra, which has twelve petals.

Having pierced the Viṣṇu-knot at its root and having meditated upon the thread or that fourth state (turya) in the center of the Anāhata-cakra, one attains non-conceptual samādhi there; then, having transcended the Anāhata,
one reaches the Viśuddhi-cakra, which has sixteen petals, and on its lower part, at the level of the penis, two side-petals are located.
At the lower portion of the Viśuddhi-cakra, there are two pieces of flesh hanging down, equal in size to the penis;
these hang down like breasts, according to another Vedic scripture which states, "That which has Indra as its source.
Leaving aside the two paths situated at its sides, one should enter the Viśuddhi-cakra through the central path of that mass of flesh.

Having entered there into the Viśuddhi [chakra], one restrains the vital breaths within the Viśuddhicakra; then, having pierced the Rudra-knot situated at its base, one enters the Ājñācakra— which is enriched by two petals— and,
moving toward or meditating upon the seed-syllable or the Fourth State (turya) in its center, one proceeds.

Having attained non-conceptual samādhi, and having tasted the nectar produced from the supreme union of the moon and sun, the yogi— whose body is free from old age and death— enters the Brahma-aperture shining with a thousand spokes; there,
he becomes the Fourth State (turya) characterized by three measures (trimātra), or rather, by fifteen measures (tripañcamātra).

That in which one finds negation is the Turyaturya; if one always perceives, "I am That," then the yogi becomes either the Turya—possessing some form based on the three measures (trimātra)—or the Turyaturya, which is formless. The word "ca" (and) serves to demonstrate the non-dual nature (niṣpratiyogikatva) of the Turyaturya.

6. He who is described as the fourth of the fourth (turyaturīya) is this very Paramahaṃsa, the Supreme Self (paramātman). Through his non-difference from the fourth state produced from his own portion, he resembles ten million suns; his radiance is like that of infinite millions of suns risen simultaneously. By means of this radiance of the fourth state, this—
The entire world is pervaded and swallowed up. || 7 ||

Through the contemplation of the *haṃsa* within the heart-lotus, there occurs the vision of the Self as the Fourth State (*turyātman*). Its activity is eightfold: on the eastern petal, the mind is inclined toward merit; on the southeast, sleep, laziness, and so forth arise; on the southern petal, the mind is inclined toward cruelty; on the southwest, the intellect is directed toward sin.

In the western direction (vāruṇī) is play; in the northwestern direction (vāyavyā) is the intellect for movement and so forth; in the northern direction (saumya) is delight in pleasure; in the northeastern direction (īśānī) is the acquisition of wealth; in the center is detachment (vairāgya). In the filaments (kesara) is the waking state;
in the pericarp (karṇikā) is dreaming; in the phallus (liṅga) is deep sleep; and upon leaving the lotus is the fourth state (turīya).
When the *nāda* has dissolved into the *haṃsa*, that is the state beyond the fourth (*turīyātīta*). Furthermore,
the *nāda* from the foundation (*ādhāra*) up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), resembling pure crystal, is indeed called Brahman, the Supreme Self.

Furthermore, for that very [Self] which has attained the state of the individual soul (*jīva*)—the locus for the superimposition of the manifold of individual distinctions—there occurs an eightfold activity consisting of eight modes. How so?
In this regard, it has been stated that the heart-lotus, which is to be presided over by that [Self], possesses twelve petals. Among those, there is a group of four petals.
Since the lotus touched by the *haṃsa*—the eight-petaled lotus of the refined ones—becomes fit for practical application, its method is now described.

In this context, the *haṃsa* is the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). When it enters the eastern petal, the mind becomes inclined toward meritorious action (*puṇya-karman*). When it enters the southeastern petal...

At that time, sleep, laziness, and so forth arise. When it enters the southern petal, the mind becomes inclined toward cruel actions. When it enters the southwestern petal, the intention to commit sinful deeds arises.
When it enters the petal situated in the western direction...

At that time, the mind becomes intent on play and diversion. When it enters the petal situated in the northwestern direction, then the intellect arises for movement, walking, and so forth. When it enters the northern petal, then delight and pleasure in the self and non-self arise for both the learned and the ignorant. When it is in the northeastern petal—
When it enters there, the thought arises of taking up objects useful for this world and the next.
When it enters into the midst of the petals, detachment from that which is other than oneself arises. When it moves within its filaments, the waking state occurs; at that time, egoism [manifests].

It attains full blossoming. When it moves within its pericarp, then one sees dreams; at that time, there is a half-blossoming of the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti). When it enters the hollow space therein, then deep sleep (suṣupti) occurs. Upon leaving the lotus characterized as described above, the fourth state (turīya) arises.
There occurs the direct realization of that. At that time, the *haṃsa* remains as the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

When the *nāda*, consisting of the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), dissolves into the *haṃsa*—the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self—then, due to the absence of the phenomenal world such as the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*) which are to be presided over by it, [the state of liberation is attained].

That which is devoid of the state of being an object superimposed by that [ignorance], which is without a substratum, beyond the fourth (turiyatita), and non-dual Brahman alone remains. (8) Thus, he says "atho" to explain how the Self of the Fourth (turyatma) shines forth in the body of the yogin distinguished by such contemplation: "atho".
Immediately following the attainment of non-conceptual samādhi, there arises within the heart of the yogin the *nāda*.
This is the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*), free from attachment due to the equilibrium of the *guṇas*, which is the fourth state (*turya*).
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*, its nature is that of the fourth state.

Brahman, which resembles pure crystal and is like a flawless mountain of crystal, consisting of white luster—that indeed is called the Supreme Self (Paramātman) who manifests within the sound (nāda). || 9 ||
The method for the recitation of the Ajapa-Hamsa mantra:
Now, *Haṃsa* is the Seer (*ṛṣi*). The unmanifest *Gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandaḥ*). The Supreme Swan (*Paramahaṃsa*) is the Deity (*devatā*).
*Haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). *Saḥ* is the power (*śakti*). *So'ham* is the pin (*kīlaka*). [This is repeated] six times.

In a day and night, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths]. "To Sūrya, to Soma, to the stainless, to the non-manifest, to the bodiless and subtle—may he impel! (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4). || 11 ||
"Vauṣaṭ to Agni and Soma"—with this [mantra], the placement on the heart and other limbs (hṛdayādyaṅganyāsa) as well as the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) are performed. || 12 ||
Having done this, one should meditate upon the self as the *haṃsa* within the heart.
The method of recitation for this mantra, which consists of the direct realization of the fourth state (turya),

is now described, together with the rites of the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), deity (devatā), and the ritual placement of limbs (aṅganyāsa), as well as meditation (dhyāna). Now, immediately after rising from bed, [the recitation is performed] according to the number of breaths counted during a day and night.

Those seeking liberation must practice the contemplation of the *ajapā* [mantra]. Therefore, inhalation and exhalation itself is called the mantra of the Self (*ātman*). Exhalation alone is the letter *sa*, which is the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*). Inhalation alone is the seed-syllable of space (*viyat-bīja*) with the nasal bindu, *haṃ*, which is the referent of the term "that" (*tat-padārtha*). The repeated union of these two is the practice.
The meaning of the term *asipada*.
The letter *sa* is declared to be Khecarī and is certainly the *tvaṃ-pada*;
the letter *ha* is the Supreme Lord and is certainly the *tat-pada*. When the living being meditates upon the letter *sa*, he shall indeed certainly become the letter *ha*.
Thus says the Śruti. Now, regarding the Ajapā-ātman mantra: *haṃsaḥ* is the seer (*ṛṣi*), who is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) itself;
the unmanifest Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*); the Supreme Haṃsa, the Supreme Self (*paramātmā*), is the deity (*devatā*); *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *saḥ*...

The power (*śakti*). I am that *kīlaka*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of the direct realization of the Self as *Haṃsa*. The six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) begins with *haṃsām* and so forth. The meditation (*dhyāna*):
[I meditate upon] that which abides in coming and going, yet is devoid of movement and the like; the singular form of consciousness, supreme and non-dual.
I bow to that Haṃsa, whose form is the Supreme Self, whom all people meditate upon as abiding within themselves.
Thus it is said.

"Oṃ, etc. refers to the fivefold worship (pañcapūjā). "So 'ham" is the mantra. Indeed, the movement of exhalation and inhalation itself is the recitation (japa). The six deities of the six bases (ādhāras), beginning with Gaṇeśa, numbering six, become the performers of the count of the recitation.
The number of breaths divided into day and night is now declared:
in a day and night there are twenty-one thousand six hundred [breaths].
Day after day, by the count of twenty-one thousand six hundred inhalations and exhalations, I am that very one.
They recite "So 'ham. Having divided the distinguished Ajapā into four parts, one should offer the first portion to Sūrya, the Virāḍ-ātman;
the second portion should be offered to Soma, who has attained the state of the Sūtra, with the mantra "Pracodayāt"; likewise the third...

The portion designated as "atanu-sūkṣma" (the non-subtle-subtle) should be applied and dedicated to the Lord of All, the Stainless One who is to be presided over by Him, acting as the substratum for the projection of the Virāṭ-sūtra.
As for the remaining fourth portion, it consists of the appearances of the gross, the subtle, and the seed-state, along with their respective presiding deities, which are distinct from oneself.

May [the mantra] dissolve—that is, cause to vanish—the vast manifold of the gross, the subtle, and so forth, into the Supreme Self, which is non-different from the inner witness and free from all appearance, by virtue of being the substratum for the negation of all portions to be discarded within Virāṭ and the other levels of manifestation. 11. *Vauṣaṭ* to Agni and Soma; [this is for] the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs, as well as the placement on the hands.

"Bhavataḥ" [is used]; "haṃsauṃ," possessing a long vowel, is used in the six cycles; "saṃsauṃ" is used in place of the fifth cycle, or otherwise, one should perform it with "agnīṣomābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ"—this is the meaning. (12) Having thus performed the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and so forth, [one should do so] in the heart.
One should meditate on the self as the swan, realizing "I am Brahman," which is non-different from the innermost reality. || 13 ||
Through meditation on the swan endowed with qualities, there is the vision of the Supreme Self:

Agni and Soma are the two wings, Oṃkāra is the head, Ukāra is the three-eyed [face], Bindu is the mouth, Rudra and Rudrāṇī are the two feet; one should fashion this twofold form from the throat—thus is the Unmanā state.
This is called the withdrawal of the *ajapā* [mantra]. (14) Thus, by means of the *haṃsa*, the mind is investigated. (15)
Thus, for one who is unable to practice meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), the method of meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) is stated:
"Agni and Soma. For the Haṃsa that has attained the state of Vairāja, Agni and Soma—the sun and the moon—become its two wings and two arms. Its head, however, is the syllable Om (Oṃkāra). Of this...
The three eyes are the syllables *A*, *U*, and *M* together with the *bindu*. Rudra is its face;

Rudrāṇī and Gaṅgā are its two feet. Thus, according to the distinction between the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*), the seeker of liberation should perform the meditation on the *haṃsa* twice, directly from the throat by means of the sound of the throat.

One should act without hesitation. Thus, by means of meditation in these two modes, the mind that has arisen is cast away; he whose such activity [is thus stilled] is the "unminded" (unmanā) sage. The *ajapā* is the *haṃsa-vidyā*;
its withdrawal or dissolution occurs within the Supreme Self, which is non-different from the inner self—this is that [state].

The withdrawal of the *ajapa* [mantra] is designated as the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Thus, by virtue of the meditation on the *haṃsa* as "I am He" (*so'ham*), one reflects upon and determines—through the negation "not this, not this" (*neti neti*)—that neither the mind nor its effects exist apart from the *haṃsa*. || 14–15 ||

Through the recitation of the *ajapā*, one experiences the resonance (*nāda*); by ten million recitations of this very [mantra], one experiences the resonance. And that arises in ten forms: the first is *ciṇiti*, the second is *ciṇiciṇīti*, and the third is the sound of a bell (*ghaṇṭānāda*).

The fourth is the sound of the conch; the fifth is the sound of the lute; the sixth is the sound of the cymbals; the seventh is the sound of the flute; the eighth is the sound of the kettle-drum; the ninth is the sound of the clay drum; the tenth is the sound of the clouds. || 16 ||
If the seeker of liberation is unable to perform meditation on the Saguna and Nirguna aspects,

then for one who performs the recitation of the *Aja-pā* Hamsa mantra— which is accomplished silently throughout day and night in the form of inhalation and exhalation— the state of the resonance (*nāda*) born of one's own experience [is attained].
He states the intermediate fruit and the supreme fruit of that contemplation [with the words] "of this very": *asyaiva* (p.

568). By the power of ten million recitations—that is, by the efficacy of reciting exactly ten million times—of this very *haṃsa-mantra* as previously described, this seeker of liberation [perceives] the *nāda-brahman* in the *anāhata-cakra*.

One experiences and knows [this] through the means of valid cognition that is one's own direct experience (*svānubhūti-pramāṇa*). This experienced sound (*nāda*) arises and is manifested in ten ways within the right ear. He describes its sequence as follows: "ciṇiti. The initial sound consists of the resonance of *ciṇiti*.
The second sound consists of the resonance "ciṇiciṇī"; the third sound is like the ringing of a bell; the fourth is manifested like the sound of a conch shell;
the fifth is manifested like the sound of the strings of a lute; and the sixth resembles the sound of cymbals.
The seventh [stage] has a sound equal to that of a sweet-sounding flute;
this eighth is like the sound of a kettle-drum; this ninth resembles the sound of a mṛdaṅga drum; and the tenth is similar to the roar of a thundercloud. || 16 ||
The method for practicing the suppression of the breath exclusively:
having abandoned the ninth, one should practice the tenth alone. || 17 ||
Thus, among the ten kinds of sounds, having abandoned those from the first up to the ninth, the seeker of liberation should practice only the tenth. || 17 ||
The fruit of experiencing those respective nādas is as follows:
in the first [stage], there is the trembling of the limbs; in the second, the breaking of the limbs;
in the third, one undergoes piercing; and in the fourth, the head shakes. (18)
In the fifth [stage], the palate flows; in the sixth, there is the enjoyment of nectar;
in the seventh, hidden knowledge; and likewise, in the eighth, the supreme speech (parāvāk).
In the ninth [state], the body becomes invisible and the divine eye likewise pure;
and in the tenth, the supreme Brahman exists in the proximity of the Self of Brahman.

p. 569) Regarding the first sound (*nāda*) called *ciṇ*, when that first sound is experienced as it truly is, then one's own body appears as *ciñciṇī*. Likewise, in the second [sound], there is the breaking of that body; but in the third, the heart undergoes piercing, [and] the heart-lotus [is likewise affected].

It attains expansion. In the fourth stage, however, one's own head shakes; the meaning is that when the wind has entered the *ājñā-cakra* during the state of *kumbhaka* for one who has ascended to the *ṣaṇmukhī-mudrā*, the head shakes. (18) In the fifth stage, when the *tantrī-nāda* is manifested, it flows from one's own palate.

Upon the manifestation of the sound of the tāla known as the sixth, there occurs the tasting of nectar— the partaking of the nectar produced from the unification of the two mandalas of the moon and the sun. Upon the manifestation of the sound of the flute, which is the seventh,
there arises the realization regarding that hidden Brahman which transcends one's own limited self and all other people.

Upon the manifestation of the sound of the eighth drum, this yogi unfolds through the supreme speech (parāvāk), which embodies all the Vedas and Śāstras; he becomes a knower of the sciences concerning all objects and attains omniscience. || 19 ||
Upon the manifestation of the sound of the ninth *mṛdaṅga*, for those who perceive the body [as such], it becomes invisible;
one becomes possessed of powers such as invisibility (*antardhāna*). One becomes a lord (*īśvara*) possessing pure divine vision and knowledge of the three times.
Through the various attainments (*siddhi*) arising from the sounds beginning with the first and ending with the ninth, there is indifference toward them.

The meaning is that, as previously stated, upon the manifestation of the tenth [letter] as Meghanāda, in the proximity of Brahman—the Self, which is non-different from the inner witness (pratyag-abhinna)—there occurs the negation of the notions of difference and unity residing therein, which had arisen through the false perception of one's own ignorance and so forth; thus, Brahman alone remains, established as that which is free from such [dualistic] conceptions. || 20 ||
From the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*), there is the manifestation of the identity with Brahman.
Therefore, when the mind has dissolved— that is, when mental constructs and fluctuations have ceased and merit and demerit have been burnt—
the Sadāśiva, whose nature is Śakti, who abides everywhere, is himself the self-luminous, pure, and awakened one.
"He is eternal, stainless, and most peaceful; he illumines"—this is the Vedic recitation;
"it comes to be"—this is the Upaniṣad. || 21 ||
But how is it that only Brahman alone remains, given the existence of the mind, its effects, volitions, merit, demerit, and so forth, which are distinct from itself? To this, he says: "Therefore.
Because this entire collection of transformations such as the mind and so on is conceptualized by one's own ignorance, therefore...
When the mind has dissolved into the mind through one's own knowledge (*svajñāna*) and reached a state of rootless extinction,

when its effects— conceptualization and discursive thought (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*)— and even their effects, merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*), have been burnt and reduced to ashes by the fire of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), then [the superimposition of] that mind distinct from oneself and its effects...
As the subject of discourse— by virtue of being the fourth-of-the-fourth (turyāturya) meaning of the *praṇava* of Brahman—

the Supreme Lord Sadāśiva, whose essence consists of all the powers inherent in each respective category of objects, abides everywhere throughout the manifest and unmanifest phenomenal world as the nature of existence,
consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). Through association with the insentient phenomenal world, He possesses the quality of insentience.

Regarding the word "syāt" (it may be), he says: "self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*). Since the insentient phenomenal world, which appears through the perspective of one's own ignorance, is false from the perspective of one's own knowledge, the inquiry into it is likewise [false]. For the Self is self-luminous, being by nature non-insentient. Therefore, this [Self] is pure, due to the absence of impure *māyā*. *Māyā*—
Lest it be argued that even that which follows after [the Self] would possess that same nature, he says: "eternal" (*nitya*). Because it is pure existence (*sattāmātra*).

Since the word "mere" (*mātra*) excludes everything else, one might think that there could still be "staining" (*añjanatā*) therein; therefore, he says: "untainted" (*nirañjana*). Since pure existence is devoid of any counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*), how could there be any staining by anything else?

Can it be established? Regarding the question, "How can there be the state of being pure existence without a counterpart when the darkness caused by one's own ignorance—the cause for the existence of what is other than oneself—is present?"—it is said: "It illuminates that which is most profoundly peaceful.
At the very moment of its realization, one reaches the state where the darkness of one's own ignorance and its effects is negated.

This very [Self] is most peaceful; for this reason, it shines forth as being without a counterpart (*niṣpratiyogika*). Regarding this point, it is said: "Even here, one perceives only Being (*sanmātra*); that which is other than this is non-existent. There is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman; whatever is other than this is perishable, for there is no non-existence apart from Brahman alone."
The final conclusion of the spiritual scriptures is indeed the negation of everything:
"In this world, there is no ignorance, nor is there illusion; this Brahman is peaceful and free from fatigue."
Thus there occurs the recitation of the Vedas and so forth. The two words "iti" and "upaniṣad" serve the purpose of marking the conclusion of the Upaniṣad. || 21 ||
This clear commentary on the Haṃsa Upaniṣad was written by Upadeśabrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra;
the explanation of the Saṃsa Upaniṣad is recorded as consisting of one hundred and seventy verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Haṃsopaniṣad, completing the fifteenth [work] in the commentary on the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the venerable Īśa.
